title: Platform Engineering in the Age of AI
gist: A five-person InfoQ Live roundtable of platform engineers (DKB, sevDesk/Shine, Harness, an independent Kubernetes consultant) argues AI shifts platform-engineering bottlenecks from code generation to the outer deployment loop (security scans, governance, approvals), forces heavier investment in reusable AI context/guardrails as a platform responsibility, and pushes toward a governed 'autonomous SDLC' rather than displacing platform jobs.

themes.theme: AI's actual impact on platform team workload

insights.claim: A platform engineering manager at sevDesk/Shine identifies three areas of AI benefit for platform teams: tactical (previously neglected but important tasks like documentation, boilerplate, recurring Infrastructure-as-Code changes across repos become cheap to do), operational (using AI to run discovery/aggregation across roughly 100 AWS accounts and hundreds of Terraform repositories), and strategic (internal MCP servers/skills let AI answer first-line developer questions, reducing support burden).
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: A concrete three-tier framework (tactical/operational/strategic) for scoping AI ROI in platform engineering that other teams can benchmark against; the ~100-account, hundreds-of-repos scale gives a sense of real enterprise Terraform sprawl.
insights.locator: Definitely, AI is already changing how platform teams

insights.claim: A DKB platform engineer argues AI does not change platform engineering fundamentals — it is a new automation tool operating at greater scale, now serving workloads from agents as well as humans, making clear service intent, scope, and APIs more important than before.
insights.speaker: Stephane Di Cesare
insights.so_what: Counters AI-hype narratives: the durable platform-engineering discipline (clear APIs, service scope) is a prerequisite for AI adoption, not something AI replaces.
insights.locator: I think what we also see is what platform engineering

insights.claim: A Harness Field CTO argues that as code-generation time drops, the bottleneck shifts to the outer loop — deployment, security scans, and governance gates — creating pressure on platform teams to enable machine-speed self-service because leadership questions why AI-generated code isn't reaching production faster.
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: Identifies CI/CD, security scanning, and approval-gate automation as the next major investment area for platform teams and vendors as AI eliminates the coding bottleneck — a clear infra-spend signal (favors CI/CD, security-scan, and governance tooling vendors).
insights.quote: It needs to operate at machine speed versus human speed.
insights.locator: One thing on top of that is, as code generation

insights.claim: A principal engineer notes AI increases pressure on open-source maintainers because AI makes it far easier for anyone to find security vulnerabilities, meaning maintainers feel perpetually behind on patching.
insights.speaker: Camila Macedo
insights.so_what: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery is outpacing maintainer patch capacity — a structural risk for the open-source supply chain that security tooling vendors could address.
insights.locator: Nowadays, AI is helping people find so many security issues

themes.theme: Guardrails, governance, and centralized AI context

insights.claim: Platform teams increasingly manage reusable AI context (code conventions, PR-creation skills, ticketing-system integration skills) as a first-class platform responsibility, alongside guardrails to prevent agents from taking excessive initiative when they hallucinate, and FinOps functions like managing AI tool licensing and token-usage overages.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: Defines a new platform-team product category — 'AI context management' plus FinOps for token spend — that internal platform teams and vendors will need to build out.
insights.locator: In terms of AI, I see a similar responsibility

insights.claim: A principal engineer states that AI does not change security fundamentals — least privilege, clear permissions, strong policy, and strong auditing apply to AI agents exactly as they do to human users, and the platform team's role is to provide common services where the risk and cost are shared organization-wide.
insights.speaker: Camila Macedo
insights.so_what: A conservative, security-first framing that treats agents as just another identity class requiring the same IAM discipline — useful pushback against AI-exceptionalism in security policy design.
insights.locator: About security, like they are saying

insights.claim: A DKB engineer states that at a bank, AI adoption is welcomed because it does not extend to letting agents make final decisions — compliance, security, and legal review remain mandatory human checkpoints, unlike a hypothetical world where an AI agent could directly alter account balances.
insights.speaker: Camila Macedo
insights.so_what: Regulated-industry adoption pattern: AI assists but does not make autonomous financial decisions, a conservative posture likely to be the norm across banking infrastructure for the near term.
insights.quote: I'm very happy that the bank is not trying to use agents to take the decisions. Because one day I can get up and see my bank account, I'm rich. The other, I'm poor, because it's not deterministic.
insights.locator: I just would like to say for Stephane

insights.claim: A panelist cites a specific accuracy statistic that Anthropic's Opus 5 benchmark shows 25% to 65% accuracy with regard to code, arguing this level of unreliability means organizations cannot yet trust AI to make autonomous decisions.
insights.speaker: Camila Macedo
insights.so_what: A concrete, if second-hand, benchmark figure (25-65% accuracy) grounding skepticism about full agent autonomy in production financial systems — useful data point for AI-reliability due diligence.
insights.quote: Anthropic from Opus 5, the benchmark is like 25% to 65% of accuracy with regards to code.
insights.locator: If you check Anthropic, for example

insights.claim: A Harness Field CTO warns that AI models can be silently updated by the third-party provider, causing unexpected behavior shifts (model drift), and that teams not regularly monitoring model responses can be caught off guard — making post-production AI evaluations and continuous monitoring critical governance practices.
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: Silent model updates from third-party AI vendors are an operational risk enterprises must monitor for via continuous evaluation pipelines — an emerging MLOps/AI-observability product requirement.
insights.quote: I've seen it where the model is changed underneath you silently.
insights.locator: I've seen it where the model is changed

insights.claim: A Harness Field CTO predicts organizations will need a fully autonomous SDLC where governance, guardrails, and evidence generation are built into the deployment pipeline itself, because a change-advisory-board that meets weekly cannot keep pace with AI-driven rates of change; he foresees agents autonomously detecting bugs, writing fixes, submitting PRs, and having other agents deploy and verify them.
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: A clear infrastructure roadmap: weekly CAB-style change approval processes are becoming obsolete, driving demand for automated governance/evidence pipelines (a product category Harness and competitors are building toward).
insights.locator: I really foresee that in the near future

insights.claim: The same speaker uses a highway-versus-freeway analogy: platform teams must build stronger, more structured pipelines (like freeways) to let development go faster and safer, arguing this governance-and-structure investment is what allows organizations to sustain machine-speed development without crashing.
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: A useful mental model for justifying continued/increased platform engineering investment even as AI writes more code — speed requires infrastructure, not just capability.
insights.locator: You think about like the highway system

insights.claim: A DKB engineer insists that even as agents become more autonomous, a human always remains behind the loop setting intent — the platform continues to serve humans through faster agents, and how autonomous an agent is allowed to be remains a human decision.
insights.speaker: Stephane Di Cesare
insights.so_what: Frames full agent autonomy as a governance dial platform teams control, not an inevitability — relevant to how enterprises will structure human-in-the-loop requirements.
insights.locator: What I think is we shouldn't forget as well

insights.claim: A panelist argues AI will not eliminate platform-engineering jobs but will eliminate toil/repetitive tasks, freeing engineers for harder governance and context-layer problems, drawing an explicit historical parallel to how compilers abstracted complexity without eliminating developer jobs.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: Pushes back on job-displacement narratives with a historical analogy (compilers), useful context for workforce-planning discussions in engineering organizations.
insights.locator: Definitely, AI will steal some of the platform work

insights.claim: A principal engineer draws the same compiler analogy independently, arguing AI is evolutionary rather than job-replacing, and that people who understand code, can maintain it, and can debug it will remain required even as AI becomes very good at generating code.
insights.speaker: Camila Macedo
insights.so_what: Two independent panelists converging on the same compiler analogy strengthens the thesis that platform/software engineering roles evolve rather than disappear under AI.
insights.locator: In the same way that the compilers didn't take

themes.theme: Measuring platform success and developer trust

insights.claim: A DKB engineer states there is no reliable objective metric for platform success; the working approach is qualitative developer trust and psychological safety, since developers historically view platform teams as an 'ops team that says no,' and building trust that the team wants developers to succeed is a long-term project.
insights.speaker: Stephane Di Cesare
insights.so_what: Reinforces that AI-era platform success metrics remain fundamentally about developer trust and qualitative feedback, not just quantitative throughput numbers — relevant for platform-team leaders building OKRs.
insights.locator: I have to say that I don't have the answer

insights.claim: A platform engineering manager measures platform success primarily through onboarding time (idea-to-production time, e.g., reducing a three-week Kubernetes/Fargate deployment setup to one hour), request volume/back-and-forth in Slack and PRs as a proxy for documentation gaps, and by proxying DORA metrics before and after platform-team formation.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: Concrete, actionable platform-success KPIs (onboarding time, DORA proxy, PR back-and-forth volume) usable as a benchmark template by other platform teams.
insights.locator: The simplest way to understand if we are really helping
